output.title: When an open-ended retainer starts to blur the work
output.body:
If you run a small business, the real issue with an open-ended retainer is not the monthly invoice. It is the work that slowly stops looking bounded.

That usually shows up in one recurring task: repeated customer questions, neglected leads, or manual invoice/data work that keeps coming back. In the persona scenario, that kind of work can take 8–10 hours a week. At that point, you are no longer asking, “Should I keep paying?” You are asking, “Is this one workflow worth automating, or should it stay manual for now?”

That is the decision we try to make concrete. First, identify one recurring workflow. Then ask whether it has a clear owner, a repeatable outcome, and a limit you can state in plain English. If the answer is fuzzy, a retainer will usually stay fuzzy too.

Bareni’s process is simple: a free 30-minute diagnostic to check whether the workflow fits, then, if it does, a fixed-price pilot with defined scope and measures. Timings are intended as scope, not a promise. The customer keeps the accounts; retainer support is optional; and human approval stays mandatory for money movement.

One practical next step: write down the single workflow, the weekly time it consumes, and one outcome you would want to see before you commit further. That gives you a cleaner conversation than “can you just keep an eye on it?”
